question: What is the point of equal time (PET)?

options.text: The point on track that is the same distance from the departure and the destination
The point on track at which half of the planned trip fuel has been used
The point on track from which it takes the same time to fly to either of two aerodromes
The point on track from which the aircraft can return to departure with no reserve fuel left

explanation: The PET (also called critical point or equal time point) is the track position from which the flying time to either of two suitable aerodromes is the same.

question: What other names are used for the point of equal time?

options.text: Point of no return or safe point
Critical point or equal time point
Top of descent or diversion point

explanation: The PET is also called the critical point (CP) or the equal time point (ETP).

question: Which two aerodromes can a PET be calculated between?

options.text: Only the destination and its nominated alternate aerodrome
Only two en route alternates lying on opposite sides of the planned track
Only the departure and destination aerodromes of the flight
Departure and destination, or any two suitably placed aerodromes

explanation: The two aerodromes can be departure and destination, or any two aerodromes suitably placed in relation to the track.

question: What is the PET used for in flight?

options.text: Deciding quickly which of two aerodromes is closer in time after a failure or emergency
Deciding where to change from true to grid navigation on a polar route
Deciding when to start the descent into the destination aerodrome on arrival at the end of the cruise
Deciding whether there is enough fuel to return to the departure aerodrome at all

explanation: After an engine or major system failure, or a medical emergency, the PET tells the pilot which aerodrome can be reached sooner.

question: Is the PET a time problem or a fuel problem?
explanation: The PET is a time problem: the times home and on are equal. The fuel loaded will always be enough to fly from the PET to either aerodrome.

question: In still air, where is the PET?

options.text: At the point of safe return
Two thirds of the way to the destination

explanation: With no wind the ground speeds on and home are equal, so the equal time point is at the halfway point.

question: With a wind, in which direction does the PET move from the halfway point?
explanation: The PET moves into wind; the stronger the wind, the greater the movement.

question: An aircraft has a headwind component on the way out. Where must the PET lie?

options.text: Less than halfway to the destination
More than halfway to the destination

explanation: The PET moves into wind. With a headwind out, the return is downwind, so the PET is beyond halfway: a useful gross error check.

question: Which formula gives the distance from the first aerodrome to the PET?
explanation: X = D × H/(O + H), where D is the total distance, O the ground speed on and H the ground speed home.

question: In the PET formula X = D × H / (O + H), what are O and H?

options.text: The ground speeds on to the destination and home to the departure
The headwind and tailwind components on the outbound track
The ground speeds outbound to the PET and back to the departure
The true airspeeds with all engines and with one engine inoperative

explanation: O is the ground speed continuing on to the second aerodrome and H the ground speed returning home to the first.

question: Having found the distance to the PET, how is the time to it found?

options.text: Divide the distance by the ground speed out to the PET
Multiply the distance by the ratio of the two ground speeds
Divide the distance by the TAS with one engine inoperative
Divide the distance by the ground speed home from the PET

explanation: Time to the PET = distance to the PET ÷ the ground speed out from departure to the PET (at the all-engine TAS).

question: The distance from A to B is 1500 NM. The ground speed on is 240 kt and home 180 kt. What is the distance from A to the PET?
explanation: X = 1500 × 180/(240 + 180) = 643 NM. The PET is short of halfway because the return is into wind.

question: The distance from A to B is 1500 NM. The ground speed on and out is 240 kt and home 180 kt. What is the time from A to the PET?
explanation: X = 643 NM; at 240 kt that takes 2.68 h = 2 h 41 min.

question: The distance from A to B is 2400 NM. The ground speed on and out is 450 kt and home 510 kt. What are the distance and time from A to the PET?
explanation: X = 2400 × 510/960 = 1275 NM; at 450 kt that takes 2 h 50 min.

question: The TAS is 420 kt and there is a 35 kt headwind component all the way from A to B, 2400 NM. What is the distance from A to the PET?
explanation: O = 385 kt and H = 455 kt. X = 2400 × 455/840 = 1300 NM, beyond halfway as expected with a headwind out.

question: The TAS is 420 kt with a 35 kt headwind component all the way from A to B, 2400 NM. What is the time from A to the PET?
explanation: X = 1300 NM, flown out at 385 kt: 3.38 h = 3 h 23 min.

question: The TAS is 380 kt with a 40 kt tailwind component from A to B, 1800 NM. What are the distance and time from A to the PET?
The distance A to B is 500 NM and the TAS 300 kt. With a 60 kt headwind on the way out, where is the PET?
explanation: O = 240 kt, H = 360 kt. X = 500 × 360/600 = 300 NM, more than halfway.

question: The distance A to B is 500 NM and the TAS 300 kt. With a 60 kt tailwind on the way out, where is the PET?
explanation: O = 360 kt, H = 240 kt. X = 500 × 240/600 = 200 NM, less than halfway.

question: TAS is 200 kt on a track of 090°(T), with a W/V of 030°/40 kt. A to B is 1000 NM. The ground speeds are 177 kt out and on and 217 kt home. What is the distance to the PET?
explanation: X = 1000 × 217/(177 + 217) = 551 NM. With a headwind component out, the PET is past halfway.

question: When the wind is not along the track, how should the ground speeds home and on be found for a PET?

options.text: By halving the wind speed and applying it as a headwind in both directions
By adding or subtracting the full wind speed from the TAS for each direction
With the navigation computer for each direction, allowing for drift on each
By using the TAS for both directions, as a crosswind has no effect on time

explanation: The ground speed out/on and home must each be found on the computer, balancing the drift for the outbound and reciprocal tracks; there is no short cut.

question: TAS is 450 kt on a track of 180°(T), with a W/V of 240°/60 kt. A to B is 2000 NM. The ground speed out and on is 417 kt and home 477 kt. What are the distance and time to the PET?
explanation: X = 2000 × 477/894 = 1067 NM; at 417 kt the time is 2 h 34 min.

question: A flight departs at 1105 UTC. The PET is 204 NM from departure and the ground speed out is 178 kt. What is the ETA at the PET?
explanation: 204/178 = 1.146 h = 1 h 09 min, so the ETA is about 1214 UTC.

question: What happens after an engine failure that affects the PET calculation?

options.text: The aircraft climbs to a higher level and flies on at the same TAS
The aircraft drifts down to a lower level and flies on at a reduced TAS
The aircraft must always return to the departure aerodrome
The aircraft continues at the same level and the same TAS as before the failure

explanation: After an engine failure the aircraft drifts down to a stabilising altitude and continues on or returns home at the lower engine failure TAS.

question: Which TAS is used to find the ground speeds home and on for an engine failure PET?

options.text: The TAS at the drift-down level with all engines
The average of the two TAS figures

explanation: For the engine failure PET distance, O and H are worked out from the engine failure TAS.

question: Which ground speed is used to find the time to an engine failure PET?

options.text: The average of the all-engine and engine failure ground speeds
The all-engine ground speed out from departure to the PET
The engine failure ground speed home from the PET to departure
The engine failure ground speed out from departure to the PET

explanation: The aircraft flies to the PET with all engines working, so the time uses the all-engine ground speed out.

question: Why is an engine failure PET normally used even for emergencies other than engine failure?

options.text: Other emergencies are not allowed for in planning
The engine failure PET always gives more fuel
The two PETs are usually very close in distance
The all-engine PET cannot be calculated in a wind

explanation: Even with a large difference between the two TAS values, the two PETs differ very little in distance, so the engine failure PET is normally constructed and used for other serious occurrences too.

question: All-engine TAS is 460 kt, engine failure TAS 360 kt, and there is a 30 kt headwind component outbound. A to B is 2600 NM. What is the distance to the engine failure PET?
explanation: Engine failure O = 330 kt and H = 390 kt. X = 2600 × 390/720 = 1408 NM.

question: All-engine TAS is 460 kt, engine failure TAS 360 kt, with a 30 kt headwind component outbound. The engine failure PET is 1408 NM from A. What is the time to it?
explanation: The aircraft flies out with all engines at 460 − 30 = 430 kt: 1408/430 = 3.27 h = 3 h 16 min.

question: All-engine TAS is 480 kt, engine failure TAS 380 kt, with a 40 kt tailwind component. A to B is 3000 NM. What are the distance and time to the engine failure PET?
explanation: Engine failure O = 420 kt, H = 340 kt: X = 3000 × 340/760 = 1342 NM. Time at all-engine GS out of 520 kt = 2 h 35 min.

question: For the same flight, all-engine TAS 480 kt with a 40 kt tailwind and A to B 3000 NM, where is the all-engine PET?
explanation: All-engine O = 520 kt, H = 440 kt: X = 3000 × 440/960 = 1375 NM, only 33 NM from the engine failure PET.

question: Ground speed on is 300 kt and home 250 kt with one engine inoperative; ground speed out with all engines is 350 kt. A to B is 1200 NM. What are the distance and time to the engine failure PET?
explanation: X = 1200 × 250/550 = 545 NM; at the all-engine 350 kt out it takes 1.56 h = 1 h 34 min.

question: If an engine fails exactly at the engine failure PET, where should the aircraft go?

options.text: To whichever has the longer runway
Either aerodrome, as the times are equal
Always on to the destination aerodrome
Always back to the departure aerodrome

explanation: At the PET the flying times to both aerodromes are equal, so in theory either can be chosen; other factors such as weather then decide.

question: An engine fails before the aircraft reaches the engine failure PET. Which aerodrome is reached sooner?
explanation: Before the PET the time home is less than the time on, so the aircraft returns; after it, continuing is quicker.
